overview: Maiasaura peeblesorum ("good mother lizard") transformed understanding of dinosaur parental behaviour. From the Late Cretaceous Two Medicine Formation of Montana (~76 Ma), nesting colonies preserving eggs, hatchlings and juveniles at different stages were discovered by Jack Horner and Bob Makela in 1978. The hatchlings' underdeveloped limb bones showed they were born helpless and required parental feeding in the nest — the first evidence of extended parental care in non-avian dinosaurs.

The Maiasaura bonebeds in Montana are extraordinary: a single catastrophic event — possibly a volcanic ashfall — killed approximately 10,000 individuals in one horizon. This mass-death assemblage across a wide area provides bone histology data for the entire population, showing Maiasaura grew at rates comparable to modern large mammals rather than reptiles.

fossilSites.note: Campanian nesting colony with multiple Maiasaura clutches at different developmental stages; the site where parental care was first recognised in dinosaurs.

articles.title: The discovery that changed palaeontology
articles.body: Jack Horner and Bob Makela described Maiasaura in 1979 from material found by Marion Brandvold near Choteau, Montana in 1978. The eggs and hatchlings showed underdeveloped legs and worn teeth — indicating the young were fed in the nest by adults for an extended period. This overturned the prevailing view of dinosaurs as indifferent egg-layers and established them as attentive parents.

articles.title: Growth rates
articles.body: Bone histology from the massive Two Medicine bonebed shows that Maiasaura grew from 50 cm at hatching to 7 metres adult length in 6–8 years — a rate comparable to modern large ungulates, not reptiles. This is now considered typical for hadrosaurs and confirms that non-avian dinosaurs had elevated metabolic rates relative to modern reptiles.

articles.title: Hadrosaur ecology
articles.body: Maiasaura was a flat-headed (non-crested) hadrosaur that lived in large herds on the coastal plains of the Western Interior Seaway. It migrated seasonally — bone evidence suggests the Two Medicine Formation records different herd stages at different times of year. The colonial nesting, where multiple females laid eggs in the same area, mirrors modern colonial nesters such as penguins.

fossilRecord.material: Eggs, nests, juveniles and adult skeletal material from nesting colonies.
fossilRecord.paleo: Late Cretaceous seasonal floodplain settings in Montana.
fossilRecord.evidence: Nesting grounds and growth series provide direct evidence for reproduction and development.

record.mya: late Campanian, about 77-75 million years ago
record.description: Maiasaura peeblesorum was a hadrosaurid from the Two Medicine Formation of Montana, documented by nesting grounds, eggs, juveniles, adults and large bonebeds.
facts: Nest colonies and very young individuals in nests show repeated nesting-site use and extended nest occupancy.
The evidence is consistent with parental care but does not specify which sex cared for young or every detail of provisioning.
Large growth-series samples document rapid growth and population structure.

review.ageReviewNote: The Two Medicine Maiasaura record is late Campanian, approximately 76.7-75 Ma.

residualUncertainty: Details of parental provisioning and social structure exceed the direct evidence.

evidence.material: Thousands of bones, many skeletons, eggs, nests and a growth series from embryos to adults.
evidence.confidenceLimit: Nesting and growth are secure; specific family roles and herd behaviour remain interpretations.
evidence.summary: Maiasaura peeblesorum was a hadrosaurid from the Two Medicine Formation of Montana, documented by nesting grounds, eggs, juveniles, adults and large bonebeds.
